title: Mathlete MTB
summary: My tutoring business and its lab of mountain-bike math tools.
description: The home of my math and physics tutoring for young athletes: the Mathlete Lab of interactive mountain-bike math tools, plus one-on-one sessions in math, physics and SAT prep.
overview: Mathlete MTB is my tutoring business, built around a simple idea: young athletes learn math faster when the problems are about something they care about. The site brings together the Mathlete Lab — interactive tools that put students on the trail, at the race desk or in the bike shop — and private one-on-one tutoring.

The Lab is organized into four themed labs: the Engineering Lab (physics, motion and mechanical systems), Trail Crew (trail design, mapping and terrain), Race Team (performance analysis and statistics) and Bike Workshop (gearing and component setup). Students can filter every tool by activity, math subject, level and time.
details: Open tools: Trail Builder, MTB Physics Playground, Gear Ratio Lab, Strava Showdown and Jump Lab.
Members-only tools for my students, including Summit Expedition.
Focus Training: math tools built on research into short attention spans, in development.
Private tutoring on Zoom with a shared whiteboard, from middle school math through Calculus, high school physics and SAT prep, with online booking.
A companion Mathlete Ski section.
thumbnailAlt: Mathlete MTB homepage: the Mathlete Lab with its Engineering Lab, Trail Crew, Race Team and Bike Workshop

title: Gear Ratio Lab
summary: Pick the gears, work the ratios, race the rival.
description: A race-mechanic game: students choose a chainring, wheel and cogs for each section of a mountain-bike course, work out the ratios, speeds and times, then race their setup against a rival's.
overview: Students play the mechanic for a mountain-bike racer. Each course section lists its grade, the rider's cadence and a push limit — the biggest gear ratio the rider can turn there. Go over it and the rider walks; every cog change costs time. Students work the numbers for every section, race their setup against a rival's on the course profile, then change one part, predict the new time and test the prediction.

The same game runs at six levels: Algebra I (ratios, rates, inequalities), Geometry (circumference, gear inches), Algebra II (inverse variation, constraints), Precalculus (angular velocity), Statistics (percent steps, spread) and Calculus (related rates).
details: Spec — pick a race course.
Plan — choose a chainring, a wheel and one rear cog per section.
Lab — work out the ratio, distance per crank turn, speed and time for every section, plus one problem for the class.
Race — the setup races the rival's on the course profile.
Tune — change one part, predict the new time, test it, and answer the mechanic's question.
thumbnailAlt: Gear Ratio Lab: choosing a math class and a race course on the mechanic's bench

title: Strava Showdown
summary: Call the podium, crunch the riders' stats, plot the race.
description: A race-analyst game: students call the podium from a field of riders' ride data, crunch each rider's stats, plot them on a distance–time graph, and defend their final call with numbers.
overview: Students sit at the race analyst's desk for a mountain-bike team. They're dealt a field of riders and a brief saying what the team is selecting for, lock in a podium prediction before doing any math, then compute each rider's stats and plot every rider on a distance–time graph, where slope is speed. The round ends with the coach's question, answered with numbers and the graph, and a final podium.

The same game runs at six levels: Algebra I (rates, d = rt, systems), Geometry (coordinate distance), Algebra II (means of rates), Precalculus (average rate of change), Statistics (spread and z-scores) and Calculus (integrals and the Mean Value Theorem).
details: Deal — a field of riders and a race brief.
Call it — predict the podium before any math; it locks in.
Crunch — compute each rider's stats on the analyst sheet, plus one problem for the class.
Plot — plot each rider on a distance–time graph.
Showdown — answer the coach's question with numbers and the graph, then give the final podium.
thumbnailAlt: Strava Showdown: choosing a math class and a race field at the analyst's desk

title: Trail Builder
summary: Build a trail on budget by solving the math for every segment.
description: A trail-crew game: students take a client's work order, solve the math for every trail segment they build, and have to land exactly on the finish elevation within budget.
overview: Students run a trail crew building real-world-inspired trails in New Zealand, Chile, Scotland, Canada and Tasmania. A client sets the budget, the trailhead elevation and where the trail must finish. Every segment bought from the shop needs its math solved before it goes in, then a test rider rides the finished trail — and flats and washouts cost money.

The same game runs at six levels: Algebra I (linear models and inequalities), Geometry (right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem), Algebra II (quadratics, exponentials, logs), Precalculus (trigonometry and angles), Statistics (probability and expected value) and Calculus (derivatives and integrals).
details: Survey — take a work order with a budget, a trailhead elevation and a finish.
Build — buy segments and solve the math for each one; the trail must end exactly at the finish elevation.
Ride — a test rider rolls the die on every segment rated 3 or higher.
Review — score up to 100 points plus a bonus, name the trail, explain why it works, and add it to the trail network.
thumbnailAlt: Trail Builder: choosing a math class, a destination and a client work order

title: HVAC Studio
summary: Residential HVAC design, from floor plan to proposal, in one model.
description: I got tired of working in outdated Wrightsoft software for HVAC design, so I'm building my own: a browser-based workspace that takes a house from floor plan to loads, equipment, ducts and proposal using one building model.
overview: Residential HVAC design usually means re-entering the same house in tool after tool. HVAC Studio is built around one idea: draw the house once, then size the system, the ducts and the proposal from that same model. Every dimension is stored to the sixteenth of an inch, and any missing engineering input stays visibly missing until someone enters it, instead of quietly falling back to a default.

The first piece, Building Studio, is working today: a 2D floor-plan editor where you draw walls and rooms, place windows and doors, and get live room area, volume and exposure by compass direction. Load analysis, equipment selection, duct design and estimates & proposals come next.
details: Building Studio: walls, rectangle, polygon and click-to-fill rooms, windows and doors, multiple floors, snapping, live dimensions and typed exact lengths.
Full thermal assemblies on walls, windows and doors, with model validation as you draw.
Import a PDF or image of existing drawings and calibrate its scale from two points.
Undo/redo, copy/paste, autosave with conflict detection, version history and crash recovery.
Accounts and organizations with owner, admin, designer, sales and viewer roles, and strict separation between companies' data.
Load figures, once added, will be labeled preliminary estimates rather than ACCA Manual J reports.
thumbnailAlt: HVAC Studio floor plan with a living room, kitchen and primary bedroom, showing the bedroom's area, volume, exposed walls and window area

title: Surface Studio
summary: Turns short writing into images of words on real surfaces.
description: An open-source studio that turns short writing into images where the words look physically written, painted, printed or traced onto a real surface — made for Substack Notes and other feeds.
overview: Text-on-image posts usually come out looking flat or, when an image model draws the words, misspelled. Surface Studio never lets an image model draw your text. Type the words, pick a surface — brick, paper, a chalkboard, a fogged window and 57 more — choose how the words go on (spray, ink, chalk, paint, print and more), then pick a composition and export.

Every image is built from three independent layers: the scene, the typography and the material. They're merged only at the end, with perspective, bends, relief and lighting tying them together. Editing the text never regenerates the scene, and changing the surface never touches the text. Every render checks that the drawn characters match your text exactly, and export refuses to write a file if they don't.
details: 61 surfaces, each rendering in four compositions, with text verified exact on every one — including punctuation, emoji, accents and CJK.
Controls for alignment, size and emphasis, material intensity and drips, lighting, mood and rotation.
Optional AI scene generation (OpenAI, Google Imagen, Replicate) produces a blank surface; you place the writing by dragging four corners.
A framework-free rendering engine and studio UI, a single-file browser prototype, and a full-stack Next.js app with SQLite storage.
27 unit tests, plus a headless Chrome harness that renders every surface in every composition.

title: Tend
summary: An iPhone app for habits, tasks and goals in one daily view.
description: A native iPhone app for habits, tasks and goals: one Today view shows the week's progress, every habit and the day's tasks, with streaks that follow your actual schedule.
overview: Most habit apps treat every habit as a daily checkbox. Tend handles the way habits actually work: drink 8 glasses of water, meditate 10 minutes, work out 3 times a week, or quit something entirely. The Today view puts a week strip with completion rings, a progress summary, every habit card and the day's tasks on one screen, with undo on everything.

All of the habit logic lives in a standalone, unit-tested Swift engine. Statuses and streaks are recomputed from the full history every time, so editing a past day always updates every number. Days are stored as calendar days rather than timestamps, so daylight saving time and travel never shift your history.
details: Five habit types: check-off, amount, times per period, measurement and quit.
Flexible schedules — daily, weekdays, every N days, N times a week or month — with partial, skipped and paused days that each affect streaks differently.
A library of 121 habit templates to search, preview and customize.
Tasks with lists, due dates, priorities, recurrence, reminders and drag-to-reorder.
A calendar with habit rings and task dots on every day.
Multiple reminders per habit that fire only on scheduled days; JSON export and import.
29 unit tests on the habit engine cover time zones, daylight saving time, weekly streaks, pauses, rule changes and relapses.
Coming soon on TestFlight.
thumbnailAlt: Tend's Today screen on an iPhone: a week strip with completion rings, 45% of the day done, and habit cards for drinking water, meditating, reading and working out

title: The Notebook
summary: A private library for the lessons and ideas I want to keep.
description: A private library for the lessons and ideas worth keeping. Every note is a page of notebook paper: capture a thought in a few seconds, scroll back through them one at a time, or lay them all out on a desk.
overview: The lessons that change how I work and live tend to get lost in random notes apps, screenshots and bookmarks. The Notebook gives them one quiet home. Each note is a page of notebook paper, and adding one takes a few seconds with Quick Capture.

Reading them back is the point. The Scroll shows one note at a time — newest first, favorites only, or shuffled — and the Library lays every note out on a desk with search, categories and favorites. New notebooks start with twelve categories, such as Mindset, Discipline, Money and Health & Fitness.
details: Your original writing can't be changed: edits are saved as revisions, and any edited note can show its original version.
Search combines ranked full-text search with partial-word matching across titles, writing, tags and categories.
Shuffle uses a seeded order, so paging through a shuffled feed never repeats or skips a note.
Each person's notes are walled off twice — in every query and in the database itself.
Export everything to Markdown or JSON; deleting your account removes everything.
Next: uploading and importing existing notes, and AI suggestions for titles, categories and tags that are always labeled and never rewrite your words.
thumbnailAlt: The Notebook Library: notes shown as pages of lined notebook paper, with search and category filters

title: Leverage Planner
summary: Ranks my tasks by leverage and fits the best into my real day.
description: A local-first planner that ranks what I could be doing by leverage against my own goals, then fits the best of it into my real day.
overview: A local-first personal strategy engine. It ranks everything I could be doing by leverage against my own goals, fits the best of it into my real day with sleep, meals, training and people protected, and compares that plan with what I'd otherwise do. Daily and weekly reviews feed back in, recalibrating time estimates and flagging when one goal is eating more than its share of the week. No accounts or API keys, and all data stays in the browser.
details: An eight-factor weighted leverage score, with a plain-language explanation for every ranking.
A scheduler that works around routine, commitments and travel, matches tasks to energy and focus windows, and stops before eating into requested open time.
Important tasks that don't fit come back with concrete fixes: postpone something lower-ranked, shorten, split or move to tomorrow.
After three completed tasks per goal, actual-vs-estimate ratios recalibrate future durations.
55 unit tests cover the scoring, scheduling, comparison and review engine.
thumbnailAlt: Leverage Planner Today view showing the three highest-leverage actions for the day
